title: Tiling a Two-Row Strip
statement:
You need to cover a strip that is 2 cells tall and n cells wide. You have unlimited pieces of two shapes:

  • a domino, 2 cells in a line, placed either upright or lying flat;
  • an L-piece, 3 cells forming an L, in any of its four rotations.

Every cell must be covered by exactly one piece, and no piece may stick out. Two tilings are different if some pair of neighbouring cells is covered by the same piece in one and by different pieces in the other.

Return the number of tilings modulo 1 000 000 007.

examples.why: Three upright dominoes; one upright plus two flat on the left or on the right (2 ways); or two L-pieces locked together, in 2 mirror images.
A single upright domino. An L-piece needs at least two columns.

The dominoes-only count would be 5. The L-pieces add 6 more: an interlocked L pair (2 ways) next to an upright domino on either side (4), plus two L-pieces at the ends with a flat domino between them (2).

hints: Fill the strip from left to right. When you stop partway, what can the right edge of the filled part look like?
Either both rows end at the same column (flat edge), or one row sticks out by one cell (jagged edge). Count tilings of each kind separately.

Let full[i] count tilings of the first i columns with a flat edge and part[i] with the top row one cell longer (the bottom case is a mirror). full[i] = full[i−1] + full[i−2] + 2·part[i−1] and part[i] = full[i−2] + part[i−1].

explain.intuition:
With dominoes alone this is Fibonacci: the last column is one upright domino or the last two are two flat dominoes. L-pieces break that, because they leave the edge jagged, with one row a cell longer than the other. So track two kinds of partial tilings: a flat edge after i columns (full[i]) and a jagged edge where one row covers i cells and the other i − 1 (part[i], one orientation).

A flat edge at i comes from: a flat edge at i − 1 plus an upright domino; a flat edge at i − 2 plus two flat dominoes; or a jagged edge at i − 1 closed by an L-piece, in either orientation. A jagged edge at i comes from a flat edge at i − 2 plus an L-piece, or a jagged edge at i − 1 extended by a flat domino in the short row. Substituting one into the other also gives the one-line recurrence f(n) = 2·f(n − 1) + f(n − 3).
pitfalls: Forgetting the factor 2: a jagged edge can stick out on the top or on the bottom row.
Treating it as Fibonacci because the first values 1, 2 look like it. n = 3 already gives 5, not 3.
Applying the modulo only at the end. The counts overflow long before n = 1000.

solutions.title: Flat and jagged edge states
solutions.idea: Count tilings that end in a flat edge and in a jagged edge separately; each feeds the other.

solutions.title: Single recurrence
solutions.idea: Eliminating the jagged state gives f(n) = 2·f(n − 1) + f(n − 3), with f(0) = 1, f(1) = 1, f(2) = 2.

followups: n is up to 10¹⁸. How do you get the answer in O(log n)? (Matrix power.)
